task_description: Drug-induced hematological toxicity prediction, including myelosuppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, pancytopenia), coagulopathy (bleeding, hemorrhage), hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, methemoglobinemia, and other blood-related adverse effects.
prediction_question: Does this molecule exhibit hematological toxicity? Your final answer should be formatted as either: 'Final answer: Toxicity' or 'Final answer: Non-toxicity'.

DHFR.role: Folate metabolism and de novo nucleotide biosynthesis in hematopoietic progenitor cells
DHFR.logic: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, the one-carbon carrier required for de novo thymidylate and purine synthesis. Depletion of tetrahydrofolate stalls DNA replication in rapidly dividing bone-marrow hematopoietic progenitors, producing myelosuppression; this is the mechanism of antifolates such as methotrexate.
DHFR.role_cited: Folate metabolism and de novo nucleotide biosynthesis in hematopoietic progenitor cells[3t]
DHFR.logic_cited: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate[3], the one-carbon carrier required for de novo thymidylate and purine synthesis[3t]. Depletion of tetrahydrofolate stalls DNA replication in rapidly dividing bone-marrow hematopoietic progenitors[4t][8!], producing myelosuppression[5t]; this is the mechanism of antifolates such as methotrexate[6].

TYMS.role: De novo thymidylate synthesis essential for DNA replication in hematopoietic lineages
TYMS.logic: Thymidylate synthase catalyzes the sole de novo route to thymidylate (dTMP), using a folate cofactor to methylate dUMP. Loss of this activity depletes the thymidine pool needed for DNA synthesis in hematopoietic lineages, producing myelosuppression; this is the mechanism of fluoropyrimidines and antifolate TS inhibitors.
TYMS.role_cited: De novo thymidylate synthesis essential for DNA replication in hematopoietic lineages[7t][8c]
TYMS.logic_cited: Thymidylate synthase catalyzes the sole de novo route to thymidylate[7t] (dTMP)[7], using a folate cofactor to methylate dUMP[7t]. Loss of this activity depletes the thymidine pool needed for DNA synthesis in hematopoietic lineages[8c], producing myelosuppression[9t]; this is the mechanism of fluoropyrimidines and antifolate TS inhibitors[10][11].

VKORC1.role: Vitamin K cycle and synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X in hepatocytes
VKORC1.logic: Vitamin K epoxide reductase regenerates reduced vitamin K, the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X in hepatocytes. Depletion of functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors prolongs coagulation and produces bleeding; this is the mechanism of coumarin, 4-hydroxycoumarin, and indanedione anticoagulants.
VKORC1.role_cited: Vitamin K cycle[12t] and synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X in hepatocytes[13t][14t]
VKORC1.logic_cited: Vitamin K epoxide reductase regenerates reduced vitamin K[12t], the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X in hepatocytes[13t][14t]. Depletion of functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors prolongs coagulation[12t] and produces bleeding[13]; this is the mechanism of coumarin, 4-hydroxycoumarin, and indanedione anticoagulants[13].

PSMB5.role: Chymotrypsin-like proteolytic subunit of the 20S proteasome governing protein turnover in megakaryocytes
PSMB5.logic: PSMB5 carries the chymotrypsin-like active site that drives the rate-limiting proteolysis of the proteasome, degrading ubiquitinated proteins such as IkB and thereby permitting NF-kB activation. In megakaryocytes this NF-kB activity is required for proplatelet formation and platelet release without affecting megakaryocyte proliferation; its loss lowers circulating platelets. This is the mechanism of proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib.
PSMB5.role_cited: Chymotrypsin-like proteolytic subunit of the 20S proteasome[15t][16t] governing protein turnover in megakaryocytes[17c]
PSMB5.logic_cited: PSMB5 carries the chymotrypsin-like active site[15][16] that drives the rate-limiting proteolysis of the proteasome, degrading ubiquitinated proteins such as IkB[18] and thereby permitting NF-kB activation[18]. In megakaryocytes this NF-kB activity is required for proplatelet formation[17!] and platelet release[17!] without affecting megakaryocyte proliferation[19]; its loss lowers circulating platelets[17c]. This is the mechanism of proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib[16][17!].

DHODH.role: De novo pyrimidine biosynthesis supplying nucleotides for DNA and RNA synthesis in proliferating cells
DHODH.logic: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is a flavin enzyme on the inner mitochondrial membrane that oxidizes dihydroorotate to orotate, the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis coupled to the respiratory chain. Depletion of uridine and cytidine nucleotides limits DNA and RNA synthesis in rapidly dividing bone-marrow progenitors, producing cytopenias; this is the mechanism of DHODH inhibitors such as leflunomide and teriflunomide.
DHODH.role_cited: De novo pyrimidine biosynthesis supplying nucleotides for DNA and RNA synthesis in proliferating cells[20t][21t]
DHODH.logic_cited: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is a flavin enzyme[22] on the inner mitochondrial membrane[23t][24t] that oxidizes dihydroorotate to orotate[22t], the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis[23t][25t] coupled to the respiratory chain[24t]. Depletion of uridine and cytidine nucleotides limits DNA and RNA synthesis in rapidly dividing bone-marrow progenitors[20t], producing cytopenias[25t]; this is the mechanism of DHODH inhibitors such as leflunomide and teriflunomide[23].

pathway_rules: Inhibition of DHFR or TYMS interrupts folate-dependent regeneration of tetrahydrofolate and de novo thymidylate synthesis, depleting the dTMP and purine nucleotides required for DNA replication in bone-marrow progenitors and producing myelosuppression.

Inhibition of DHODH halts de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis, depleting uridine and cytidine nucleotides needed for DNA and RNA synthesis in rapidly dividing hematopoietic progenitors and producing cytopenias.
Inhibition of VKORC1 blocks regeneration of reduced vitamin K, impairing gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and prolonging coagulation, which increases hemorrhagic risk.
Inhibition of PSMB5 suppresses proteasomal proteolysis and downstream NF-kB signaling in megakaryocytes, blocking proplatelet formation and platelet release and producing thrombocytopenia.

Hematotoxic drugs act either by carrying a DNA-reactive or antimetabolite pharmacophore that damages dividing progenitors, or by potently inhibiting the nucleotide, coagulation, or proteasome targets above; the majority of therapeutic agents carry neither liability and spare the marrow at clinical exposure.

yes_features: Aromatic amine in which an amino, hydroxylamino, or nitroso nitrogen is bonded directly to an aromatic ring carbon; oxidative bioactivation to nitrenium and nitroso species covalently modifies marrow progenitors and neutrophils, linked to agranulocytosis and hemolytic anemia.

Aryl sulfonamide bearing a sulfonyl S(=O)(=O) group joined to an amine on an aromatic ring; bioactivated to reactive hydroxylamine and nitroso metabolites associated with idiosyncratic agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia.

Nitro group attached directly to an aromatic ring; nitroreduction yields nitroso and hydroxylamino intermediates that damage hematopoietic progenitors, the archetype being chloramphenicol-associated aplastic anemia.
Alkylating warhead such as a nitrogen mustard, aziridine, epoxide, or alkyl sulfonate ester that covalently crosslinks DNA and arrests division of hematopoietic progenitors.

Nucleoside or nucleotide analog in which a purine or pyrimidine base is attached to a ribose, deoxyribose, or acyclic sugar-mimetic linker; it is incorporated into or blocks nucleic acid synthesis in dividing hematopoietic cells.
Antifolate pharmacophore built on a 2,4-diaminopteridine or 2,4-diaminopyrimidine that inhibits DHFR or TYMS and blocks folate-dependent nucleotide biosynthesis.

Planar polycyclic system of three or more fused fully aromatic rings such as acridine, anthracene, or an anthracycline aglycone that intercalates DNA and disrupts replication in dividing hematopoietic cells.
Coumarin, 4-hydroxycoumarin, or indanedione motif that antagonizes vitamin K-dependent coagulation and increases hemorrhagic risk.
no_features: Endogenous or nutrient-like small metabolite such as an amino acid, sugar or polyol, short-chain alcohol, or simple carboxylic acid that is processed by normal intermediary metabolism.

Fused non-aromatic sterane nucleus of a corticosteroid, glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, sterol, or bile acid; its saturated rings cannot intercalate DNA and it acts through nuclear-hormone-receptor signaling rather than marrow injury.
Secosteroid or vitamin-D-like scaffold with an opened, flexible seco ring that is non-aromatic and cannot intercalate DNA.

Single benzene ring carrying only metabolically stable substituents such as ethers, alcohols, aliphatic amines, simple amides, or aliphatic halogens, with no aromatic amine, aryl sulfonamide, or aromatic nitro group.
Benzodiazepine, GABAergic, or local-anesthetic-type central-nervous-system scaffold lacking any DNA-reactive or redox-active substituent.

Selective aminergic G-protein-coupled-receptor ligand of the adrenergic, serotonergic, or muscarinic classes built on a phenethylamine or arylpiperidine core without an alkylating or redox-active group.
Saturated cage or aliphatic hydrocarbon amine such as an adamantane derivative that has no aromatic ring and none of the reactive alerts above.
Highly polar, high-TPSA, zwitterionic, or peptide-like molecule with poor passive membrane permeability that limits bone-marrow and progenitor exposure.

contradiction_flags.segment_text: Depletion of tetrahydrofolate stalls DNA replication in rapidly dividing bone-marrow hematopoietic progenitors,
contradiction_flags.mla: Koury, M. J., and D. W. Horne. "Apoptosis Mediates and Thymidine Prevents Erythroblast Destruction in Folate Deficiency Anemia." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, vol. 91, no. 9, 1994, pp. 4067-71. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.91.9.4067.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: Apoptosis of erythroblasts in the late stages of differentiation leads to decreased erythrocyte production and to anemia. The increased erythropoietin produced in response to the anemia increases the number of erythroid progenitor cells in the differentiation stages preceding those in which the cells undergo apoptosis.
contradiction_flags.note: The clause locates the lesion as replication arrest in progenitors; the source locates it as apoptosis of late-stage differentiating erythroblasts with expansion, not stalling, of the progenitor pool. The shared upstream element (reduced thymidylate synthesis) means the disagreement is about the affected cell stage and failure mode, not about folate's role. (That tetrahydrofolate depletion stalls DNA replication in rapidly dividing bone-marrow hematopoietic progenitors.; Folate-deficient erythroid cells proliferated and differentiated to late erythroblast stages and then died by apoptosis, while erythropoietin expanded the preceding progenitor stages.)

contradiction_flags.segment_text: In megakaryocytes this NF-kB activity is required for proplatelet formation and platelet release
contradiction_flags.mla: Shi, Dallas S., et al. "Proteasome Function Is Required for Platelet Production." The Journal of Clinical Investigation, vol. 124, no. 9, 2014, pp. 3757-66. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI75247.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: The failure to produce proplatelets in proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes was due to upregulation and hyperactivation of the small GTPase, RhoA, rather than NF-κB, as has been previously suggested.
contradiction_flags.note: The paper names NF-kB as the previously suggested mechanism and rejects it in favour of RhoA/ROCK, which is directly incompatible with NF-kB being required for proplatelet formation. The genetic work is murine; human megakaryocytes were also used for the proplatelet assays. (That NF-kB activity in megakaryocytes is required for proplatelet formation and platelet release.; Failure of proplatelet formation in proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes was due to RhoA upregulation and hyperactivation rather than NF-kB, and ROCK inhibition rescued it.)

contradiction_flags.segment_text: NF-kB activity is required for proplatelet formation
contradiction_flags.mla: Shi, Dallas S., et al. "Proteasome Function Is Required for Platelet Production." The Journal of Clinical Investigation, vol. 124, no. 9, 2014, pp. 3757-66. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI75247.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: The failure to produce proplatelets in proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes was due to upregulation and hyperactivation of the small GTPase, RhoA, rather than NF-κB, as has been previously suggested.
contradiction_flags.note: Refuted-hypothesis pattern: the clause restates a proposal this paper tested and rejected, and the quote names NF-kB explicitly (rendered NF-kappaB in the raw record). The incompatibility is direct. (That NF-kB activity is required for proplatelet formation.; Proplatelet failure under proteasome inhibition was mediated by RhoA hyperactivation rather than NF-kB, as previously suggested.)

contradiction_flags.segment_text: This is the mechanism of proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib.
contradiction_flags.mla: Shi, Dallas S., et al. "Proteasome Function Is Required for Platelet Production." The Journal of Clinical Investigation, vol. 124, no. 9, 2014, pp. 3757-66. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI75247.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: The failure to produce proplatelets in proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes was due to upregulation and hyperactivation of the small GTPase, RhoA, rather than NF-κB, as has been previously suggested.
contradiction_flags.note: The recorded quote supports the clause on any reading (it affirms proteasome function is critical for thrombopoiesis in bortezomib-treated patients). What the abstract refutes is the segment's NF-kB step, and the RhoA sentence is the one that does that work. (That the preceding (NF-kB-dependent) step is the mechanism by which proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib act on platelet production.; Proteasome function is critical for thrombopoiesis, but the effector is RhoA/ROCK signaling, not NF-kB.)

contradiction_flags.segment_text: Inhibition of PSMB5 suppresses proteasomal proteolysis and downstream NF-kB signaling in megakaryocytes,
contradiction_flags.mla: Shi, Dallas S., et al. "Proteasome Function Is Required for Platelet Production." The Journal of Clinical Investigation, vol. 124, no. 9, 2014, pp. 3757-66. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI75247.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: The failure to produce proplatelets in proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes was due to upregulation and hyperactivation of the small GTPase, RhoA, rather than NF-κB, as has been previously suggested.
contradiction_flags.note: The NF-kB limb of the clause is what the paper set out to test and rejected. Two caveats to keep: the paper contests NF-kB's causal role in proplatelet formation rather than measuring NF-kB suppression as such, and its genetic model deletes PSMC1, not the PSMB5 subunit the clause names (the pharmacologic arm does cover PSMB5 inhibition). (That PSMB5 inhibition suppresses proteasomal proteolysis and downstream NF-kB signaling in megakaryocytes.; In proteasome-inhibited megakaryocytes the operative downstream change was RhoA upregulation and hyperactivation, explicitly not NF-kB.)

contradiction_flags.segment_text: Aryl sulfonamide bearing a sulfonyl S(=O)(=O) group joined to an amine on an aromatic ring;
contradiction_flags.mla: Lehmann, David F. "The Metabolic Rationale for a Lack of Cross-Reactivity Between Sulfonamide Antimicrobials and Other Sulfonamide-Containing Drugs." Drug Metabolism Letters, vol. 6, no. 2, 2012, pp. 129-33. PubMed, https://doi.org/10.2174/187231212804096664.
contradiction_flags.contradicting_quote: Accordingly, xenobiotics that do not contain an arylamine cannot generate this reactive intermediate and do not cross react with sulfonamide antimicrobials.
contradiction_flags.note: The source does oppose treating the sulfonamido group as the hazard, but only for the non-arylamine subset of the clause's substructure; for arylamine-bearing sulfonamides it affirms the liability. It also addresses hypersensitivity cross-reactivity, not blood dyscrasias directly. (That an aryl sulfonamide substructure (sulfonyl joined to an amine on an aromatic ring) is the liability-conferring feature.; That the arylamine group, oxidized by CYP2C9 to a nitroso intermediate, is the necessary feature, and that xenobiotics without an arylamine cannot form it and do not cross-react with sulfonamide antimicrobials.)
contradiction_flags.scope: only sulfonamido-containing drugs that lack an arylamine (thiazides, celecoxib and similar); arylamine sulfonamides such as sulfamethoxazole retain the liability, and the endpoint is hypersensitivity cross-reactivity rather than hematotoxicity
